passage: I am Zeenat, and I used to think feedback meant pointing at what was wrong, loudly, so nobody could miss it. In our second year, I led the design team for the college fest, and Dilnaz kept sending posters with the text too small to read from the stage. Once I said so in the group call, in front of eleven people. She went quiet and her posters got worse. Later I messaged her privately. I said the colours were lovely, that the date line was hard to read from the back row, and asked if she'd try a bigger size. She sent a new version that evening. Same work, same me. What changed was where and how I said it. I'm still learning that part, honestly.

qa.q: How many people were on the group call when Zeenat criticised the posters?
qa.a: There were eleven people on the group call.

qa.q: What was Dilnaz probably feeling after being corrected in front of everyone?
qa.a: She was probably embarrassed and defensive, which fits her going quiet and sending worse posters, though she may also have simply been discouraged about the work.

qa.q: What could Zeenat do differently the next time a poster is not readable?
qa.a: She could tell the person privately soon after, name the specific problem such as the small date line, and suggest a fix.

qa.q: How might Zeenat see the public correction now?
qa.a: Zeenat seems a little regretful, seeing that saying it in front of eleven people made things worse while the same feedback worked in private.

grounding: Zeenat recounts a public rebuke that produced defensiveness and a private, specific note that worked.

passage: I was at the next desk in the library when Jomon leaned over to Avni and spoke quietly. I couldn't hear all of it, but I saw him hold up her draft and point at one paragraph. He said something about the second example being unclear, then slid a sticky note across with a suggestion written on it. Avni read it, tucked her hair behind her ear and nodded. Ten minutes later she was typing again, and at one point she laughed and showed him her screen. I don't know what either of them was really thinking. She might have been secretly hurt. But she stayed and worked with him, and he didn't seem to be showing off. Compared with last month, when someone shouted at her over the whole lab, it looked easier to take in. 🙂

qa.q: What did Jomon slide across to Avni?
qa.a: He slid a sticky note with a suggestion written on it.

qa.q: What might Avni have been feeling as she read the note, and what else could it have been?
qa.a: She was most likely receptive, since she nodded and started typing again, but the observer admits she might have been secretly hurt.

qa.q: What made Jomon's way of giving feedback easier to take?
qa.a: He spoke quietly, pointed to one paragraph, and offered a written suggestion, so the feedback was private, specific and usable.

qa.q: How does the observer's view of the two situations differ?
qa.a: The observer sees the quiet desk-side feedback as easier for Avni to absorb than the shouting she got in the lab last month, though they only guess at her inner state.

grounding: An observer describes specific, private, respectful feedback between peers and its calmer reception.

passage:
Monday. In the project meeting, Hemant's section of the report was missing again. Seema lost patience. "Hemant, you're dragging everyone down. Every week, same story." The room went silent. Hemant turned red and said, "Maybe if you explained things properly." They didn't speak for two days.
Wednesday. Seema caught him alone near the library. "I'm sorry about Monday. I shouldn't have said that in front of everyone." Hemant shrugged. She went on: "Your data section was due on the 10th and the 17th, and both came in after the group deadline. I'm worried about Friday's submission. Could you send me a draft by Thursday noon, even rough, so I can help?" Hemant was quiet, then said, "I've been stuck on the graphs. I didn't want to say."
Friday. His section came in Thursday at eleven, with a note: "Graphs okay now? Thanks for asking properly."

qa.q: When did Seema ask Hemant to send a draft?
qa.a: By Thursday noon.

qa.q: What was Hemant feeling after Seema's comment in Monday's meeting?
qa.a: He was embarrassed and defensive, turning red and snapping back that she hadn't explained properly.

qa.q: What changed in Seema's feedback on Wednesday, and why did it work?
qa.a: She gave it privately, apologised for the public rebuke, used specific dates and a clear suggestion, so Hemant felt safe to admit he was stuck.

qa.q: What would change if Seema had repeated the rebuke in Friday's meeting?
qa.a: Hemant would likely have become more defensive, and the problem with the graphs might never have come out.

grounding: Shows a young adult moving from a public rebuke to private, specific, respectful feedback with a suggestion, which works better.

passage: Raghav, you're a team lead now, so let your Noor didi tell you about my first month leading the design team at twenty-two. We had a junior, Imtiaz, who kept missing the colours in the client's brand guide. One day, in front of eight people, I held up his poster and said, "Did you even open the guide?" He stared at the table. After that he stopped asking me anything, and his work got worse, not better. My manager called me in. "What did you want him to learn?" she asked. "To check the guide." "Then tell him that, alone, with an example." So I did. I sat with Imtiaz and said, "On these two posters the blue was lighter than the guide's code. Could you keep the guide open next to your screen?" He nodded, and asked me three questions I'd never heard him ask. The next poster was perfect.

qa.q: How many people were there when young Noor held up the poster?
qa.a: Eight people.

qa.q: How did Imtiaz seem to feel after the public rebuke?
qa.a: He seemed ashamed and defensive, staring at the table and then stopping asking young Noor anything.

qa.q: What turning point in the story changed how young Noor gave feedback?
qa.a: Her manager's question about what she wanted Imtiaz to learn, which led her to give private, specific feedback with a suggestion.

qa.q: How did young Noor's manager see the public rebuke?
qa.a: She seemed to see it as missing the point, asking what Noor actually wanted Imtiaz to learn and pointing her to private, specific feedback.

grounding: Shows a young adult learning that private, specific and respectful feedback works better than a public rebuke.

passage: The pitch to the city council was in twenty minutes, and the office printer had jammed. Sarika was reprinting while flicking through Jagdish's slides on her phone. His slide six had a figure that contradicted slide two, and the council's engineer would spot it. Everyone was rushing around; the room was loud. She could have called across the room, "Jagdish, your numbers are wrong!" Instead she walked over and quietly said, "Two minutes? Just us." They stepped into the corridor. "Slide six says 40 buses, slide two says 34. The engineer will ask. I think 34 is right from the survey. Could you fix six before we go in?" Jagdish checked and groaned. "You're right. Thanks for not shouting it." He fixed it in a minute. In the meeting, the engineer did ask about the buses, and Jagdish answered without a stumble.

qa.q: How many buses did slide two say?
What was Jagdish feeling when he saw the mistake?
qa.a: He was dismayed, groaning at the error, and relieved and grateful that Sarika hadn't shouted it across the room.

qa.q: What made Sarika's feedback work under time pressure?
qa.a: She gave it privately and quickly, with the exact slides, the likely correct number and a clear request to fix it.

qa.q: What would change if Sarika had called out the error across the room?
qa.a: Jagdish might have felt embarrassed in front of everyone and become defensive, wasting precious minutes before the pitch.

grounding: Shows a young adult giving private, timely and specific feedback under pressure instead of a public rebuke.

passage: In the cramped office of the college magazine in Kolkata, Neelam waited until the others had left for lunch before pulling up a chair beside Ojas. That morning, in the team meeting, his layout had been late again, and Soumya had said loudly, "Some of us actually meet deadlines." Ojas had gone red and not spoken for the rest of the meeting. Neelam didn't want to repeat that. "Can I give you some feedback on the layouts?" she asked. Ojas shrugged, arms crossed. "The last two issues reached the printer a day after the deadline. On Monday they charged us extra for the rush." She paused. "Your designs are the best part of the magazine. What if we set your deadline two days earlier and I check in on Wednesday?" Ojas uncrossed his arms. "The real problem is I get the final photos late. Can the photo team send them by Tuesday?" Neelam wrote it down. "Yes. Let's fix that first."

qa.q: When did Neelam talk to Ojas?
qa.a: After the others had left for lunch.

qa.q: How did Ojas feel after Soumya's comment in the meeting?
qa.a: Ojas felt humiliated and hurt, going red and silent, and was still defensive later, arms crossed.

qa.q: What made Neelam's feedback more useful than Soumya's?
qa.a: It was private, specific about the two late issues and the rush charge, included honest praise and a suggestion, and invited his side, which uncovered the late photos.

qa.q: What would have changed if Neelam had rebuked Ojas in the meeting too?
qa.a: Ojas would likely have grown more defensive and silent, and the real cause, the late photos, might never have come out.

grounding: It illustrates a young adult giving a team member private, timely feedback with specific examples and a suggestion, in contrast to a public rebuke.
